item.title: Python 3.15 Made UTF-8 the Default on Windows, and 82% of Characters Come Back Wrong in 3.14 With No Error
item.description:
Python 3.15 came out on 9 October, and on Windows it changes what open() does when you do not name an encoding. Python 3.14 and earlier use the ANSI code page, which is cp1252 on a US or Western European machine. Python 3.15 uses UTF-8 on every platform (PEP 686). R made the same move in R 4.2.0, in April 2022 (Kalibera). So I wrote six names from R on Windows 11, one per CSV file, and read them back with Python’s csv module and no encoding argument, under 3.14.10 and 3.15.2, the current release of each.

people <- c("Nguyễn Thị Minh Khai", "Zoë O’Brien", "Łukasz Wójcik",
            "Müller", "東京", "José Álvarez")
for (i in seq_along(people)) {
  write.csv(data.frame(id = i, name = people[i]), sprintf("person_%d.csv", i),
            row.names = FALSE)
}

Under Python 3.14:

import csv

for i in range(1, 7):
    try:
        with open(f"person_{i}.csv", newline="") as f:  # no encoding argument
            print([row["name"] for row in csv.DictReader(f)][0])
    except UnicodeDecodeError as e:
        print("UnicodeDecodeError on byte", hex(e.object[e.start]))
## Nguyá»…n Thá»‹ Minh Khai
## ZoÃ« Oâ€™Brien
## UnicodeDecodeError on byte 0x81
## MÃ¼ller
## UnicodeDecodeError on byte 0x9d
## UnicodeDecodeError on byte 0x81

The same code under Python 3.15:

## Nguyễn Thị Minh Khai
## Zoë O’Brien
## Łukasz Wójcik
## Müller
## 東京
## José Álvarez

Python 3.14 returned 3 names wrong and raised on the other 3. Nguyễn, the most common Vietnamese surname and mine, came back as Nguyá»…n. Python 3.15 read all 6 correctly.

The error was luck

The three names that raised have one thing in common. Their UTF-8 bytes include one of the five byte values that cp1252 leaves undefined. Every other byte maps to some character, so cp1252 reads almost anything without complaint.

undefined = []
for b in range(256):
    try:
        bytes([b]).decode("cp1252")
    except UnicodeDecodeError:
        undefined.append(hex(b))
print(undefined)

for ch in ["Á", "á", "”", "’"]:
    b = ch.encode("utf-8")
    try:
        shown = b.decode("cp1252")
    except UnicodeDecodeError:
        shown = "raises"
    print(ch, b.hex(" "), "->", shown)
## ['0x81', '0x8d', '0x8f', '0x90', '0x9d']
## Á c3 81 -> raises
## á c3 a1 -> Ã¡
## ” e2 80 9d -> raises
## ’ e2 80 99 -> â€™

Capital Á ends in 0x81 and raises. Lowercase á becomes Ã¡ and does not. The closing curly quote ends in 0x9D and raises, while the apostrophe becomes â€™. So whether Python 3.14 warns you depends on which letters happen to be in the file.

To see how often the error comes, I sent every assigned non-ASCII character in Unicode 17.0.0, all 159,706 of them, through Python 3.15’s default writer and Python 3.14’s default reader. Not one came back right. 82% came back wrong without an error, and the other 18% raised.

Characters Count Wrong, no error Raises
Latin-1 Supplement (é, ü, ñ) 96 95% 5%
Latin Extended-A (Ł, ő, š) 128 92% 8%
Vietnamese (Latin Extended Additional) 256 92% 8%
Greek 135 94% 6%
Cyrillic 256 92% 8%
Arabic 256 92% 8%
General Punctuation (curly quotes, dashes) 111 53% 47%
CJK Unified Ideographs 20,992 85% 15%
Hangul Syllables 11,172 84% 16%
Emoji (U+1F300 to U+1FAFF) 1,895 80% 20%

The other direction is the mirror image. Python 3.14 can write only 123 of those characters, the non-ASCII part of cp1252, and raises UnicodeEncodeError on the rest. Python 3.15 raised UnicodeDecodeError on all 123 of the ones it could write. A cp1252 byte next to plain ASCII is never valid UTF-8, so the only escape is two or more non-ASCII characters in a row that happen to spell a UTF-8 sequence, such as Ã followed by ©, which reads as é.

Old files fail loudly in new Python. New files fail quietly in old Python.

Where R and Python meet

R has written UTF-8 on Windows since 4.2.0, so most of what 3.15 changes is Python catching up with R. I ran the common handoffs both ways, with the same names, under both versions.

Path Names Python 3.14.10 Python 3.15.2
R write.csv() to Python csv module all six UnicodeDecodeError right
R write.csv() to Python csv module three cp1252 can hold wrong, no error right
Python 3.15 csv.writer to Python csv module three cp1252 can hold wrong, no error right
R write.csv() to pandas.read_csv() all six right right
Python csv.writer to R read.csv() all six UnicodeEncodeError, file holds 0 of 6 rows right
Python csv.writer to R read.csv() three cp1252 can hold wrong, no error right
Python print() to R system2() all six UnicodeEncodeError right
R writeLines() to Python subprocess.run(text=True) all six stdout is None right
cp1252 file to Python csv module three cp1252 can hold right UnicodeDecodeError
cp1252 file to pandas.read_csv() three cp1252 can hold UnicodeDecodeError UnicodeDecodeError
UTF-8 file with a BOM to csv.DictReader three cp1252 can hold KeyError KeyError

Python 3.15 fixed every handoff with R. Three rows are worth a second look.

pandas did not change. read_csv() has always assumed UTF-8, whatever the locale, so it read R’s file correctly under both versions and has been raising on cp1252 files for years.

The subprocess failure hides. On Windows, subprocess.run() decodes the child’s output in a background thread. When the decode fails, that thread prints a traceback, run() returns normally, and stdout is None (line 1682 of subprocess.py in 3.14.10). check=True does not catch it, because R exited cleanly. The same line is still in 3.15.2, which works here only because its decode succeeds.

3.15 does not fix the BOM. Files saved with the “UTF-8 with BOM” option start with three marker bytes. Plain UTF-8 keeps them as an invisible character on the first column name, so row["name"] raises KeyError under both versions. Naming the encoding fixes this row and the cp1252 one:

for path, enc in [("bom.csv", "utf-8"), ("bom.csv", "utf-8-sig"), ("ansi.csv", "cp1252")]:
    with open(path, newline="", encoding=enc) as f:
        header, first = f.readline(), f.readline()
    print(f"{path:9} {enc:10}", repr(header.split(",")[0]), first.split(",")[0])
## bom.csv   utf-8      '\ufeffname' Zoë O’Brien
## bom.csv   utf-8-sig  'name' Zoë O’Brien
## ansi.csv  cp1252     'name' Zoë O’Brien

What to change

Name the encoding everywhere. open(path, encoding="utf-8") and subprocess.run(..., encoding="utf-8") behave the same on every version and every machine. Python 3.10 and later can flag each call that leaves it out, as the call runs:

with open("person_1.csv") as f:
    f.read()
with open("person_1.csv", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.read()
## warn.py:1: EncodingWarning: 'encoding' argument not specified
##   with open("person_1.csv") as f:

Only the first open() is flagged. If you share files with someone still on 3.14, the switch that gives 3.14 the new behavior has existed since 3.7. PYTHONUTF8=1 in the environment, or -X utf8 on the command line:

## Nguyễn Thị Minh Khai
## Zoë O’Brien
## Łukasz Wójcik
## Müller
## 東京
## José Álvarez

That is Python 3.14 reading the same six files with -X utf8.

What this does not show

  • One Windows 11 machine with cp1252 as its ANSI code page. Machines set to Japanese, Chinese, or other code pages fail in different ways, and I did not test them.
  • I wrote the cp1252 and BOM files as bytes rather than saving them from Excel or Notepad.
  • The large table counts single characters. A file raises if any one character raises, so long Chinese or Korean text raises more often than its row suggests, and a short Western name list raises less.

What to do on Monday

  1. Search for open( without encoding=, or run your tests once with -X warn_default_encoding.
  2. Pass encoding="utf-8" to open(), Path.read_text(), and subprocess.run().
  3. Read files that may start with a BOM with encoding="utf-8-sig".
  4. Read old ANSI exports with encoding="cp1252", on purpose.
  5. Until everyone is on 3.15, set PYTHONUTF8=1 on the machines that are not.

R code on Windows needs no change for 3.15, because R got here first. Files from colleagues still on 3.14 are the exception: read those with read.csv(fileEncoding = "cp1252"). How CSV, Parquet, and other formats carry text and types between tools is covered in the data formats chapter of Advanced Data Analysis. The audit script, encoding_audit.py, sits next to this post.

item.title: Polars 2.0 Row Order: The Same Query Returned a Different Answer on Every Run
item.description:
Polars 2.0 shipped on 6 October, and its headline change is that collect() on a lazy query now runs on the streaming engine. The announcement gives row order as one reason that needed a major version, and the upgrade guide is clear that the streaming engine does not guarantee row order for joins, group-bys, and similar operations. What it cannot tell you is what that does to code written when order happened to hold. So I ran the same queries, with default settings, under Polars 1.44.2 (the last 1.x release) and 2.1.0 (the current release, out on 25 October). 2.0.0 gave the same results in every run I made before 2.1.0 shipped.

Query 1.44.2: runs wrong of 20 2.1.0: runs wrong of 20 2.1.0: distinct answers
first purchase per customer 0 20 20
running total per customer 0 20 20
dedupe, keep first 0 20 20
row index, first 1,000 0 20 20
head(20) 0 0 1

Under 1.44.2 every query matched its explicit-order version on every run. Under 2.1.0, 4 of the 5 were wrong on every one of the 20 runs, and for those 4 no two runs agreed with each other. The code did not change. Only the version did.

The data are two tables written to Parquet from R: 2,000,000 purchases in time order and 100,000 customers.

library(arrow)
set.seed(20261030)
n_cust <- 100000L
n_ev <- 2000000L
customers <- data.frame(customer_id = 0:(n_cust - 1L),
                        segment = sample(c("a", "b", "c", "d"), n_cust, TRUE))
# An event log in time order, so event_id is also the order of purchases
events <- data.frame(event_id = 0:(n_ev - 1L),
                     customer_id = sort(sample.int(n_cust, n_ev, TRUE) - 1L),
                     amount = round(rgamma(n_ev, shape = 2, scale = 20), 2))
events_path <- file.path(tempdir(), "events.parquet")
customers_path <- file.path(tempdir(), "customers.parquet")
write_parquet(events, events_path)
write_parquet(customers, customers_path)

The audit joins them, runs five queries whose answer depends on row order, and compares each run with the same query written so the order is explicit. The same file runs under both versions.

# Run order-dependent Polars queries with default settings and compare each
# result with the same query written so the order is explicit.
import hashlib

import polars as pl


def queries(events, customers, explicit):
    if explicit:
        j = events.join(customers, on="customer_id", how="left", maintain_order="left")
    else:
        j = events.join(customers, on="customer_id", how="left")   # the default
    return {
        "first purchase per customer":
            j.group_by("customer_id").agg(pl.col("amount").first()).sort("customer_id"),
        "running total per customer":
            j.with_columns(running=pl.col("amount").cum_sum().over("customer_id"))
             .sort("event_id").select("event_id", "running"),
        "dedupe, keep first":
            j.unique(subset="customer_id", keep="first").sort("customer_id")
             .select("customer_id", "event_id"),
        "row index, first 1,000":
            j.with_row_index("i").filter(pl.col("i") < 1000)
             .select("event_id").sort("event_id"),
        "head(20)":
            j.head(20).select("event_id").sort("event_id"),
    }


def audit(events_path, customers_path, runs):
    ev, cu = pl.scan_parquet(events_path), pl.scan_parquet(customers_path)
    truth = {k: q.collect(engine="in-memory")
             for k, q in queries(ev, cu, explicit=True).items()}
    result = {"polars": pl.__version__, "runs": runs, "queries": {}}
    for name, ref in truth.items():
        wrong, outputs = [], set()
        for _ in range(runs):
            out = queries(ev, cu, explicit=False)[name].collect()     # default engine
            outputs.add(hashlib.sha256(out.write_csv().encode()).hexdigest())
            wrong.append(0 if out.equals(ref) else 1)
        result["queries"][name] = {"runs_wrong": sum(wrong), "distinct": len(outputs)}
    return result
res2 = audit(r.events_path, r.customers_path, runs=20)

How much is wrong

ev, cu = pl.scan_parquet(r.events_path), pl.scan_parquet(r.customers_path)
truth = {k: q.collect(engine="in-memory")
         for k, q in queries(ev, cu, explicit=True).items()}
first_wrong, total_rows, total_err, index_wrong = [], [], [], []
for _ in range(10):
    got = {k: q.collect() for k, q in queries(ev, cu, explicit=False).items()}
    a = got["first purchase per customer"]["amount"]
    first_wrong.append(int((a != truth["first purchase per customer"]["amount"]).sum()))
    d = (got["running total per customer"]["running"]
         - truth["running total per customer"]["running"]).abs()
    total_rows.append(int((d > 1e-6).sum()))
    total_err.append(float(d.max()))
    picked = set(got["row index, first 1,000"]["event_id"].to_list())
    index_wrong.append(1000 - len(picked & set(truth["row index, first 1,000"]["event_id"].to_list())))

Not much, which is the problem. Across 10 runs, the first purchase came back wrong for between 7 and 12 of the 100,000 customers. A share that small passes every eyeball check. The running totals were wrong on between 153 and 282 of the 2,000,000 rows, but a wrong one was off by as much as 1,212, in a column where the median purchase is 34. The row index was the loud failure: of the first 1,000 rows, between 961 and 1,000 were different rows from the ones 1.44.2 picked.

A small test fixture does not hide it. The same first-purchase query on synthetic logs of different sizes, 10 runs each:

import numpy as np

def first_purchase_errors(n_events, runs=10, seed=1):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    n_c = max(n_events // 20, 10)
    c = pl.LazyFrame({"customer_id": np.arange(n_c)})
    e = pl.LazyFrame({"event_id": np.arange(n_events),
                      "customer_id": np.sort(rng.integers(0, n_c, n_events)),
                      "amount": rng.gamma(2.0, 20.0, n_events).round(2)})
    q = queries(e, c, explicit=False)["first purchase per customer"]
    ref = queries(e, c, explicit=True)["first purchase per customer"].collect(engine="in-memory")
    return n_c, [int((q.collect()["amount"] != ref["amount"]).sum()) for _ in range(runs)]

scale = {}
for n in [1_000, 10_000, 100_000, 1_000_000, 10_000_000]:
    n_c, bad = first_purchase_errors(n)
    scale[n] = [n_c, min(bad), max(bad), sum(b > 0 for b in bad)]
    print(f"{n:>10,} events  {n_c:>7,} customers  wrong in {scale[n][3]:>2}/10 runs, "
          f"{min(bad)} to {max(bad)} customers")
##      1,000 events       50 customers  wrong in 10/10 runs, 3 to 6 customers
##     10,000 events      500 customers  wrong in 10/10 runs, 2 to 7 customers
##    100,000 events    5,000 customers  wrong in 10/10 runs, 3 to 8 customers
##  1,000,000 events   50,000 customers  wrong in 10/10 runs, 5 to 8 customers
## 10,000,000 events  500,000 customers  wrong in 10/10 runs, 28 to 44 customers

On a thousand rows the error reaches up to 12% of the customers, so a test that compares output with a stored answer fails on every run. On ten million rows it is 28 to 44 customers out of 500,000.

Why it happens

The streaming engine splits the data into chunks and works on them in parallel. Operations that do not need order, such as a join, may hand chunks on in whatever order they finish. first(), cum_sum(), unique(keep="first"), and with_row_index() all read the order they are given, so they inherit the shuffle. head(20) came through intact here, but nothing promises that it will.

None of this is a bug. A Polars issue opened in November 2024 set out that left-join order should not be guaranteed, since it had only ever been an implementation detail, and the upgrade guide says the same thing about the new default. Code written against 1.x could rely on an order Polars never promised, and 2.0 is the first release whose default engine stops providing it.

The fix is one argument

import time

def first_q(join_order=None, expr=pl.col("amount").first()):
    if join_order:
        j = ev.join(cu, on="customer_id", how="left", maintain_order=join_order)
    else:
        j = ev.join(cu, on="customer_id", how="left")
    return j.group_by("customer_id").agg(expr).sort("customer_id")

ref = truth["first purchase per customer"]
variants = {
    "default": lambda: first_q().collect(),
    "join(maintain_order='left')": lambda: first_q("left").collect(),
    "sort_by inside the expression":
        lambda: first_q(expr=pl.col("amount").sort_by("event_id").first()).collect(),
    "collect(engine='in-memory')": lambda: first_q().collect(engine="in-memory"),
}
plan = [k for k in variants for _ in range(20)]
np.random.default_rng(7).shuffle(plan)           # interleave, so timing is fair
secs = {k: [] for k in variants}
wrong = {k: 0 for k in variants}
most = {k: 0 for k in variants}
for k in plan:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    out = variants[k]()
    secs[k].append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
    wrong[k] += int(not out.equals(ref))
    most[k] = max(most[k], int((out["amount"] != ref["amount"]).sum()))
for k in variants:
    print(f"{k:31s} wrong {wrong[k]:>2}/20   worst run {most[k]:>2} customers   "
          f"median {np.median(secs[k]):.3f} s")
## default                         wrong 20/20   worst run 14 customers   median 0.028 s
## join(maintain_order='left')     wrong  0/20   worst run  0 customers   median 0.028 s
## sort_by inside the expression   wrong  0/20   worst run  0 customers   median 0.035 s
## collect(engine='in-memory')     wrong 17/20   worst run  1 customers   median 0.044 s

Asking for order worked. Keeping the left table’s order in the join and putting sort_by() inside the expression both returned the right answer on all 20 runs. The join fix ran about as fast as the default here (median 0.028 against 0.028 seconds), so on this data it costs nothing. sort_by() is the more robust of the two, because the answer no longer depends on any upstream step keeping order.

Going back to the old engine was not enough. The upgrade guide offers collect(engine="in-memory") to restore the previous default, and it does restore the engine. It did not restore the order: on a Parquet source, 17 of the 20 runs still came back wrong, by at most 1 customer. Neither engine promises order, so the fixes that hold are the ones that ask for it. One more caution from the tracker: an optimizer bug that dropped maintain_order=True when a head() sat between a group-by and a sort (issue 30079) is fixed in 2.1.0, so upgrade before relying on maintain_order=True in that pattern.

Will your tests catch it?

from polars.testing import assert_frame_equal

bad = first_q().collect()
print("same shape:", bad.shape == ref.shape, "  same schema:", bad.schema == ref.schema)
## same shape: True   same schema: True
try:
    assert_frame_equal(bad, ref, check_row_order=False)
except AssertionError as err:
    print(str(err).splitlines()[0])
## DataFrames are different (value mismatch for column "amount")

A test that compares output with a stored answer will catch it, even one that ignores row order, because the values themselves differ. A test that checks shape, schema, or column names will pass.

R users are in the same position

data.table works through rows in the order it holds them, so amount[1L] by customer is the first purchase. DuckDB, which runs in parallel like the streaming engine, documents that first() can be non-deterministic without an ORDER BY. Same file, same question:

library(data.table)
library(DBI)
ev <- as.data.table(events)
truth_r <- ev[order(event_id), .(amount = amount[1L]), by = customer_id][order(customer_id)]

con <- dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
duck <- function(agg) dbGetQuery(con, sprintf(
  "SELECT customer_id, %s AS amount
   FROM read_parquet('%s') e LEFT JOIN read_parquet('%s') c USING (customer_id)
   GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY customer_id",
  agg, normalizePath(events_path, "/"), normalizePath(customers_path, "/")))$amount

engines <- list(
  "data.table, amount[1L]" = function()
    as.data.table(customers)[ev, on = "customer_id"][
      , .(amount = amount[1L]), by = customer_id][order(customer_id)]$amount,
  "DuckDB, first(amount)" = function() duck("first(amount)"),
  "DuckDB, first(amount ORDER BY event_id)" = function() duck("first(amount ORDER BY event_id)"))
r_res <- t(sapply(engines, function(f) {
  bad <- replicate(20, sum(f() != truth_r$amount))
  c(runs_wrong = sum(bad > 0), most_customers_wrong = max(bad))
}))
dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
r_res
##                                         runs_wrong most_customers_wrong
## data.table, amount[1L]                           0                    0
## DuckDB, first(amount)                           17                    1
## DuckDB, first(amount ORDER BY event_id)          0                    0

DuckDB without an ORDER BY was wrong on 17 of 20 runs, and with one it was right on all of them. The rule is the same in every parallel engine: if the answer depends on order, say so in the query.

What this does not show

  • The data are a synthetic event log on one machine with 16 threads. How many rows go wrong depends on the thread count and on how the engine splits the work.
  • Polars 1.44.2 being right on every run shows what it did, not what it promised.
  • head(20) was right here. Nothing guarantees that either.

What to do on Monday

  1. Search lazy pipelines for first(), last(), cum_sum(), unique(keep=...), with_row_index(), and head() downstream of a join or a group-by.
  2. Add maintain_order="left" to the join that feeds them, or put sort_by() inside the expression.
  3. Do not count on engine="in-memory" to bring the old order back.
  4. Keep one test that compares output with a stored answer. check_row_order=False is fine.
  5. In SQL, write first(x ORDER BY t) or arg_min(x, t).

Whether someone else can rerun your pipeline and get your numbers is the replication standard, covered in A Guide on Data Analysis. The two scripts used here, audit.py and run_audit.py, sit next to this post.
